items.title: nixos/boot: hint nixos-rebuild build-vm-with-bootloader

items.content_html:
When useBootLoader, useDefaultFilesystems and systemd-boot are used build an image holding only the ESP instead of a full system disk image.

Previously whenever useBootLoader was set it would cause a full disk image to be built, when in reality, all that was needed for the test was having a real bootloader.

A full system disk image embeds the whole closure, so it is about 1.3 GB and rebuilds on any closure change. The ESP image is 44 MB and changes only with the kernel, initrd or boot loader. Across the systemd-boot tests this drops the built images from roughly 32 GB to 1.1 GB.

  • Tested on my systemd nightly (v262) CI on x86_64-linux and aarch64-linux.
  • Tested on all tests in nixpkgs which would be affected (useBootLoader && useDefaultFilesystems && systemd-boot.enable) on x86_64-linux.

items.content_html:
Motivation and summary

Simple mistakes like forgetting a ; when writing nginx configs can take down all your sites.

This is because the nginx -t test command is being executed in the preStart of the systemd service. Moving this check to build time avoids these accidental small down times.

Fixes #35395.

Prior work

This has been attempted previously in #205561, but it caused some issues and was reverted in #209075.
The main issues were nginx -t being impure: it tried to access the internet to resolve hosts, and tried to read SSL certificates on the disk, which are not available in the nix sandbox.

(A gixy check was added in #57979, it makes the config fail to build if it finds security issues, but it doesn't detect syntax errors.)

Implementation

To combat the previous issues, I created an nginx patch that adds a new -S flag, which behaves like -T, but is skips the impure checks.

Testing

Manually tested this with our config which has proxyPass option with a remote domain that requires internet access to resolve, and of course we have SSL certificates. Syntax validation passes with the current config, and fails with eg. removing a ;.

I'd be happy to add automatic tests, but not sure what's the best approach. The problem is NixOS tests are for runtime asserts, some lib tests that I've met are eval time, what about build time assertions? Is a bash script (with eg. expect) next to the nginx NixOS test preferred, or converting the build time failure to eval time with IFD (I know it's disallowed for regular uses, not sure about tests)?

Description of changes

While profiling NixOS rebuilds, I noticed that build-composefs-dump.py takes a measurable amount of time (around 100ms). If a user has etc as overlayfs enabled, the script is executed every time they modify anything in /etc. I think this makes it significant enough to want to avoid this delay, so I rewrote the script in Rust. The new implementation closely mirrors the previous one and it has exactly the same output. On my machine with 180 entries in /etc, it takes less than 10ms.

I took inspiration from switch-to-configuration-ng and includes the source directly in nixpkgs next to its package.nix. The package includes NixOS tests for etc as overlayfs which the old python script didn't.

Possible disadvantages:

  • The package must be present to rebuild a system (556KB vs. 7KB for the old script assuming python is present)
  • This script may not be appropriate to be included as a package
  • May be harder to read or modify

I've been daily driving this successfully for a few months and got the idea to upstream it. I'd really appreciate feedback.

@nikstur (original author of build-composefs-dump.py)

Container runtimes like Docker and Podman disable the unshare system call as a security precaution. A hard-coded use of unshare prevents repart-image from working in such sandboxed environments.

This change lets consumers opt out from remapping the root user on the kernel side. It should be safe to disable if the image only uses userspace tools, but may break images using kernel-space filesystem drivers like btrfs.

Note: I'm not quite sure how to test this option without introducing too much duplication. nixos/tests/appliance-repart-image-verity-store.nix builds successfully with useUnshare = false, but we probably want to test building an image with it enabled as well.

items.content_html:
When stub-ld was first merged, there were some significant issues caused by the build closure size, which were ultimately mostly solved by #398449, though this was obviously a sub-optimal solution.

While studying the newly-hooked-up minimal bootstrap chain, I realized the M2 compiler from stage0-posix had everything I actually needed to make the stub-ld executables, including for i686 binaries on x86_64 systems, with zero additional build closure beyond what was already needed for stdenv.

Effectively reverts:

  • #398449
  • #457909

On the systems supported by stage0-posix (which includes everything built by hydra):

  • Makes no use of secondary nixpkgs instantiations, keeping eval costs small.
  • Shares its build closure completely with stdenv (even if it didn't, it could be bootstrapped in a few seconds). This is the case even when building the i686 binary on x86_64 systems.

On other systems:

  • Uses pkgsStatic, as it did before this PR.

Closes #373776

items.title: [WIP] Test nixos-rebuild --build-host

items.content_html:
Adds a NixOS module for T3 Code:

services.t3code = {
  enable = true;
  user = "alice";
};

Upstream ships t3 service install, which turns on linger, installs a pinned t3 from npm into ~/.t3/runtime, and runs it under a launcher that updates itself. Not quite what we want from a Nix-installation. This module runs t3 serve straight from the store as a system unit with User=, using the same kill and OOM settings as upstream's unit. Remote self-update requests are disabled, because the server isn't running under upstream's launcher.

  • user is required. Agents act with that user's repositories and provider credentials, so a dedicated system user makes no sense. State lives in the user's ~/.t3, which the t3 CLI uses too.
  • host defaults to 127.0.0.1 (same as upstream) and port to 3773. openFirewall is available for remote access.
  • Telemetry (PostHog) is off by default through T3CODE_TELEMETRY_ENABLED = mkDefault "false".
  • t3 serve creates a one-time admin pairing token on every start and prints it, with a QR code, to stdout. LogFilterPatterns keeps it out of the journal. Users pair with t3 auth pairing create instead. The token expires after 5 minutes, and upstream has no way to turn it off yet.
  • Provider CLIs come from the existing package overrides, e.g. package = pkgs.t3code.override { enableClaude = true; }.

The VM test waits for the "server is ready" log line, not only for the port to open. Upstream accepts TCP connections before its HTTP handler is attached, and requests sent in that window are never answered: pingdotgg/t3code#12215.

cc @iamanaws @qweered as t3code maintainers: this adds passthru.tests.nixos to the package. Happy to add you as module co-maintainers if you want to be.

AI disclosure: the module, test were drafted with Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5) and reviewed by me, this description being proof-read too. The commits carry Assisted-by: trailers. The upstream behavior relied on here (unit template, default bind address, telemetry switch, startup pairing token, self-update gating, startup race) was checked against the shipped 0.0.40 bundle and reproduced locally and in the VM test.

dufs is already packaged in Nixpkgs, but there is no NixOS module, so anyone serving files with it writes their own systemd unit. Public configurations that do this commonly run dufs with allow-all and an open firewall.

This adds services.dufs. With services.dufs.enable = true and nothing else, dufs serves /var/lib/dufs read-only on 127.0.0.1:5000, the firewall stays closed, and uploads and deletes are off.

New module nixos/modules/services/network-filesystems/dufs.nix, registered in nixos/modules/module-list.nix:

  • servePath, bindAddresses and port are typed options. Everything else goes in settings, which is free-form dufs YAML. Writing serve-path, bind or port into settings is an assertion failure, so each of those has exactly one source.
  • Authentication belongs in environmentFile as DUFS_AUTH, which keeps credentials out of the Nix store. settings.auth still works but warns, because the generated YAML is world-readable in the store.
  • The service runs as a dedicated dufs system user and group. /var/lib/dufs is created as a StateDirectory with mode 0750. Any other servePath must already exist and be accessible to that user; the module does not chown a directory the user chose.
  • systemd hardening: ProtectSystem = "strict", PrivateDevices, PrivateTmp, NoNewPrivileges, MemoryDenyWriteExecute, LockPersonality, RestrictNamespaces, RestrictRealtime, RestrictSUIDSGID, kernel/clock/cgroup/hostname protection, and RestrictAddressFamilies. AF_NETLINK is in that list because dufs enumerates local interfaces before it binds. A port below 1024 gets CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE and nothing else; any other port gets an empty capability set.
  • openFirewall is opt-in. TLS and reverse proxying are left to the existing nginx, Caddy and ACME modules.

maintainers/maintainer-list.nix gains a font44 entry, which the module, test, and dufs package name in meta.maintainers. The existing package maintainer remains listed. nixos/doc/manual/release-notes/rl-2611.section.md gets a new-module entry.

nixos/tests/dufs.nix is registered in nixos/tests/all-tests.nix and wired into passthru.tests in pkgs/by-name/du/dufs/package.nix. It has two nodes:

  • safe enables the module and nothing else. It checks the health endpoint answers, a file is readable, PUT and DELETE are refused, port 5000 listens on loopback only, the other node cannot reach it, the state directory is dufs:dufs mode 0750, and the hardening properties are really set on the unit.
  • authenticated binds 0.0.0.0:80 with openFirewall, an environmentFile holding one read-only and one read-write account, and uploads and deletes enabled. The test walks MKCOL, PUT, PROPFIND (207), GET, MOVE and DELETE as the read-write account and checks each one is refused for the read-only account; anonymous and wrong-password requests get 401; cap_net_bind_service is present for port 80; uploaded files are dufs:dufs mode 600; a file survives systemctl restart dufs.service; and the password appears in none of ExecStart, the unit, the journal, or the generated YAML.

Related: #458096
